beats.headline: Why does your Spring Boot pod keep crashing?
beats.subline: It isn't just the code. It is how you define your K8s manifest.
beats.narration: Running a single container is easy. Running twelve microservices across a cluster is where things break. If your JVM crashes, it's usually because you ignored how K8s handles resources.

beats.title: The Workload Hierarchy
beats.subtitle: Deployment manages ReplicaSets, which manage Pods

nodes.label: ReplicaSet
nodes.detail: Ensures exact Pod count is running

nodes.label: Pod
nodes.detail: The atomic unit; shares network & storage

beats.narration: You never run pods alone. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, which ensure your desired pod count stays active. If a node dies, the controller schedules a new pod elsewhere.

beats.title: Production-Ready Manifest
beats.code:
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
      containers:
        - name: order-service
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "2048Mi"
            limits:
              memory: "2048Mi"
          env:
            - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
              value: "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0"

steps.explanation: Gives the JVM time to drain connections before SIGKILL.
Set requests equal to limits to prevent OOM eviction.
MaxRAMPercentage ensures the heap stays within K8s limits.

beats.narration: Set memory requests equal to limits to avoid OOM eviction. Use MaxRAMPercentage so the JVM respects the container's memory boundary, and always define a grace period for clean shutdowns.

beats.title: CPU Limits: The Silent Killer
beats.narration: Avoid hard CPU limits. They trigger CFS throttling, which freezes your JVM threads even if the node is idle. Use requests for scheduling, but leave limits off to allow for burst capacity.

beats.narration: That's the deployment foundation. In Part 2, we tackle health probes and why checking your database in a liveness probe is a recipe for a crash loop.

beats.headline: Is your database check killing your pods?
beats.subline: Health probes are the most common cause of Java outage cycles.
beats.narration: If your liveness probe checks the database, a simple network blip will kill every pod in your cluster. Let's fix your health strategy.

beats.title: The Probe Lifecycle
beats.subtitle: Separate startup, liveness, and readiness

nodes.label: Startup
nodes.detail: Wait for JVM boot and migrations

beats.narration: Startup probes protect slow JVM boots. Liveness checks if the process is dead. Readiness controls traffic flow. Never mix them up.

beats.title: Correct Probe Config

steps.explanation: High threshold for slow Spring context startup.
Check only the JVM state, not the DB.
Check if the app is ready for traffic.

beats.narration: Use the Actuator probes. Keep liveness focused on the JVM process itself. If the database is down, the app should stay alive and return a 503, not restart.

beats.title: Graceful Termination
beats.caption: Why you need a preStop hook

lines.text: # Add a delay to drain connections

beats.narration: K8s removes pods from load balancers asynchronously. Without a preStop sleep, your pod receives SIGTERM while traffic is still arriving. Add a 10-second sleep to drain connections gracefully.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Use Startup probes for slow boots
Add preStop sleep for zero downtime

beats.narration: That's the health and shutdown strategy. In Part 3, we look at why your secrets aren't actually secure and how to manage configuration properly.

beats.headline: Your K8s secrets are not encrypted.
beats.subline: Base64 is encoding, not security. Here is how to actually protect your keys.
beats.narration: If you think K8s secrets are safe, think again. They are just base64 encoded strings. Anyone with read access can decode them in a heartbeat.

beats.title: Config vs Secrets
beats.narration: ConfigMaps are for public settings. Secrets are for keys, but they are plain text in etcd. You must encrypt them at rest or use a sidecar to pull them from a vault.

beats.title: Dynamic Config Refresh

steps.explanation: Mounts ConfigMaps as files that refresh automatically.

beats.narration: Don't use env vars for everything. Mount your ConfigMaps as volumes. Spring Boot can watch these files and refresh your configuration without restarting the pod.

beats.title: Production Secret Management
beats.subtitle: Don't store secrets in Git
beats.narration: Use the External Secrets Operator. It pulls credentials from a real vault and injects them into K8s. Your Git repo remains clean and your keys remain secure.

beats.headline: Stop copy-pasting your YAML.
beats.subline: Helm is the industry standard for managing multi-environment deployments.
beats.narration: If you have separate folders for dev, staging, and prod, you are doing it wrong. Helm templates allow you to manage one chart for every environment.

beats.title: Helm Architecture
beats.subtitle: Templates + Values = Manifests
beats.narration: Helm uses Go templates. You define your deployment once, then use values files to override replicas, memory, or profiles per environment.

beats.title: Parameterized Deployment
beats.code:
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: {{ .Values.image.repo }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}

steps.explanation: Scale up or down via values file.
Promote the same image across environments.

beats.narration: Notice the double braces. This allows you to promote the exact same container image from dev to prod, just by changing the values file.

beats.title: Deploying with Helm
beats.caption: One command to rule them all
beats.narration: Upgrade your entire stack with one command. Helm handles the diff, the rollout, and the history, making rollbacks as simple as a single command.
